A 10% annual chance is not a 50% five-year chance: chart repeated events and the cash distribution

Five charts separate annual probability, multi-year event counts, expected cash cost, percentile costs and the effect of dependence on a fixed starting reserve.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Test a fixed annual event chance across several years

Interactive planning lab

Chance of at least one event in the selected window: independent years40.95%
Expected cumulative cash cost: a probability-weighted average$1,500
Chance the selected starting reserve covers all modeled costs91.85%

Original hypothetical probability model, not an observed loss rate, insurance quote or recommended reserve. Each year has at most one event, the same independently chosen marginal event probability and the same cash cost. The main distribution assumes statistical independence across years. All cash is available at the start, and event costs only reduce it: no saving, replenishment, interest, inflation, income interruption, borrowing or insurance recovery is included. Reserve coverage means total modeled cost is at most the entered cash balance. The separate fully linked stress has either no events or an event in every year, with the same annual marginal probability. Neither dependence structure is estimated from evidence.

The central idea

A small annual probability can accumulate across years, while an expected cost still leaves outcomes above it. The probability model and the cash available need separate checks.

01

State the event and the window before using a percentage

Suppose a deliberately simplified plan assigns a 10% event chance to each year, for five years. Each event costs CAD 3,000, and there can be at most one event in a year. The default calculation assumes one year’s event does not change the probability in any other year.

These are chosen teaching assumptions. They are not estimates for a car, house, job, health condition or insurance policy. A real plan would need evidence about the event definition, frequency, severity and dependence before attaching a probability to it.

The question “Will at least one event occur over five years?” differs from “How many events will occur?” Both differ from “How much cash should be available before the first bill?” The five charts keep these questions distinct.

02

Calculate the chance of no event, then take its complement

If the annual event probability is 10%, the chance of no event in a year is 90%. Under the independence assumption, the chance of no event throughout five years is 0.9⁵ = 59.049%. The chance of at least one event is therefore 1 − 0.9⁵ = 40.951%.

Multiplying 10% by five gives 50%, but that is not the probability of at least one event. The simple sum does not account for overlap among the annual-event possibilities. It also becomes impossible as a probability when a longer horizon takes it above 100%.

The curve shows the complement calculation across horizons. At 20 independent years with the same 10% assumption, the at-least-one probability is about 87.84%. It remains below 100%, rather than becoming the 200% produced by multiplication.

03

One or more events is not the same as exactly one

The NIST statistical handbook’s binomial reference gives the event-count probability formula and its cumulative distribution. The independent fixed-probability example here calculates every count from zero through five.

The default probabilities are 59.049% for zero events, 32.805% for exactly one and 8.146% for two or more. The last two groups add to the 40.951% at-least-one probability.

A reserve that pays one event can therefore cover more cases than a zero-event reserve while still leaving some repeated-event cases unfunded. For longer windows the chart combines five or more events into one display bar; its coverage calculation continues to use the full individual-count distribution.

04

The CAD 1,500 expected cost is an average across outcomes

The expected event count is years × annual probability: 5 × 0.10 = 0.5. Multiplying by CAD 3,000 gives an expected five-year cost of CAD 1,500.

No modeled path actually incurs half an event. Possible costs are CAD 0, CAD 3,000, CAD 6,000 and further whole-event multiples through CAD 15,000. CAD 1,500 is the probability-weighted mean of those outcomes, not a fractional bill or a promise about what this household will pay.

If CAD 1,500 were the only starting cash available, it would not pay one CAD 3,000 event. In this model it covers total costs only in the zero-event cases, with 59.049% probability. The expected cost can help describe a distribution without being a sufficient amount for a particular adverse outcome.

05

A percentile cost is a threshold in a discrete distribution

The default 90th-percentile cumulative cost is CAD 3,000. Zero or one event costs at most that amount and has cumulative probability 91.854%. Because event counts are whole numbers, the threshold jumps past 90% rather than providing exactly 90% coverage.

The 95th-percentile cost is CAD 6,000. The cumulative probability of no more than two events is 99.144%, while the preceding CAD 3,000 threshold covers only 91.854%.

These are model percentiles, not confidence intervals for an estimated probability, guarantees or reserve recommendations. The bounded maximum, CAD 15,000, assumes one CAD 3,000 event in each of five years. Actual emergencies can include multiple events in a year, changing costs and other expenses outside this model.

06

Coverage assumes the full reserve exists before any event

The reserve input is cash available at the start of the entire window. Every event reduces it. There are no later contributions, investment returns, reimbursements or borrowing. Since modeled outflows only accumulate, a path is covered throughout the window exactly when its total cost does not exceed that starting balance.

At the default CAD 3,000 reserve, the model covers zero or one event and reports 91.854% coverage. It does not say which year an event arrives or what a household could save before then. A plan that rebuilds the reserve after use requires a separate dated cash-flow model.

The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s emergency-fund guidance emphasizes having accessible money for unexpected expenses and distinguishing them from occasional expenses that can be budgeted. This page’s original probability example does not replace that wider household review.

07

The same annual chance can hide a different pattern of repeated costs

The independent-year model is only one possible dependence structure. The separate fully linked stress uses a single all-or-none indicator: with 90% probability there are no events in any year; with 10% probability there is one event in every year.

Each individual year still has a 10% marginal event probability. Expected total cost remains CAD 1,500. Yet the chance of at least one event is now 10%, and the five-year cost is either CAD 0 or CAD 15,000. Its 95th-percentile cost is CAD 15,000, compared with CAD 6,000 under independence.

This extreme illustration shows why annual probabilities and an expected cost do not determine the whole loss distribution. It is not a claim that real emergencies follow an all-or-none process. Weather, health, employment and asset condition may introduce dependence, changing probabilities or severity that require more suitable evidence and modeling.

08

Use the probability calculation to improve the planning questions

  1. Define the event and the period the probability describes.
  2. Separate an observed frequency from an independently chosen stress assumption.
  3. Check whether years can reasonably be treated as independent and equally risky.
  4. Inspect zero, one and multiple-event outcomes rather than only their mean.
  5. Match each relevant cash cost with money available before its payment date.
  6. Review rebuilding capacity, insurance, cost changes and other household risks separately.

Changing the horizon or annual chance in the matrix changes the at-least-one calculation. Changing cash cost scales the modeled bills; changing the starting reserve changes how many costs it can cover. None of those controls turns a selected probability into a verified fact about a household.
